scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Blues dancing originated from dances brought to America by enslaved Africans, combining sub-Saharan traditions with European immigrant elements.
Following the post-Reconstruction era, dance steps became secularized and focused on partner connection.
W. C. Handy documented early blues performances around 1905, and by 1914 premiered 'Saint Louis Blues'.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Originally tied to spiritual and religious expressions among enslaved Africans, the dances shifted after Reconstruction to express secular pleasure, affection, and sexuality between partners in close physical contact.
Today it is a living tradition.
on_screen: Footage — MISSING (use images)

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: The dance features an athletic, grounded posture with weight held on the balls of the feet, knees bent, hips pushed back, and chest forward.
Movement is polycentric and asymmetric, utilizing multiple rhythms and articulated torso isolations.
Signature movements include the Fish Tail (figure-eight hip rotations), Snake Hips (alternating forward and back knee movements keeping feet together), and Slow Drag.
Watch for Fish Tail, Snake Hips, Slow Drag.
on_screen: Hero video full screen, 30–45 s (QTvK7a-OQHQ)
Captions name each signature move as it appears
Formation: Paartanz (partner dance), close or open embrace, sometimes staying in one spot ('Dance on a Dime').

scenes.title: Listen
narration: Blues dancing is danced to blues music in a 4/4 meter, with a tempo typically ranging between 20 and 25 measures per minute (80 to 100 BPM).
Early instrumentation featured battered string instruments and guitars.
Listen for the Battered string instruments, Guitars.
The pulse is 4/4 at about 80 beats a minute.
A haunting or slow melodic structure featuring battered string instruments and rhythmic tension, sometimes incorporating a tango-style introduction before transitioning into a blues style.

Listen later: Saint Louis Blues — W. C. Handy; Slow Drag Blues — Dabney's Band

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Historical settings included southern juke joints, Chicago venues where slow dragging took place through the 1940s, and New York's Savoy Ballroom, where specific rules governed close embraces and lascivious movements.

Reconstruction imagery allowed only from the costume notes, labelled 'reconstruction'

scenes.title: The people
narration: Key figures include W. C. Handy, Mura Dehn (documentarian of 'The Spirit Moves'), Albert Murray (essayist who coined 'blues-idiom dance'), Sugar Sullivan, Snowden, Earl Snakehips Tucker, and Ken 'Snakehips' Johnson.

Regional styles include southern plantation and juke joint dances, Chicago slow dragging through the 1940s, and the European modal interpretation of 'Stehblues' or 'Tanzblues' taught in dance schools after World War II.

Rooted in sub-Saharan African dance traditions and influenced by European-British immigration, blues dancing shares a lineage with jazz dances, influencing and being influenced by the Lindy Hop and Charleston.

scenes.title: Family tree
narration: Blues dancing is sibling of Lindy Hop: Shared roots in African-American jazz dances; Lindy Hoppers danced slow versions to blues music.
Blues dancing is sibling of Charleston: Popular African-American vernacular dance from a similar historical era.
Blues dancing is precursor of Foxtrot: Slow versions of the foxtrot influenced early 20th-century slow drag and blues dancing styles.

scenes.title: Common mistakes and what to avoid
narration: A loss of coolness and control places one squarely outside the tradition; in the Savoy Ballroom, laszive movements and enge Haltung (close posture) were not tolerated.
Teachers of this dance warn against: doing the drum hit too hard and hurting your knees
